questions.q: In the market-making worked example (quoting 99.95 bid / 100.05 ask, filling 1,000 shares on each side), how much spread does the market maker capture, and does it depend on predicting price direction?
options: $1,000, and yes, it requires correctly predicting the stock's direction
$100, captured without taking any directional view at all
$0, because market making never generates profit from the spread
$10,000, based purely on predicting the stock will rise
questions.explain: (100.05 - 99.95) x 1,000 = $100, captured simply by buying at the bid and selling at the ask on offsetting customer flow — no directional prediction required.

questions.q: What is 'inventory risk' for a market maker?
options: The risk of running out of physical goods to sell
The risk of ending up net long or net short because one side of the quote gets hit far more than the other
The risk that bid-ask spreads will narrow over time
The risk of a limit order never being filled
questions.explain: Inventory risk is the real risk a market maker manages day to day — not predicting direction, but managing the position that builds up from uneven order flow on the two sides of the quote.

questions.q: In the mental-math drill — short 500 shares at $80, stock drops to $76.50 — what is the P&L and why?
options: A loss of $1,750, because short positions always lose when price falls
A profit of $1,750, because a short position gains when price falls: (80 - 76.50) x 500
A profit of $500, ignoring the price change entirely
A loss of $500, based on share count alone
questions.explain: A short position profits when price falls; entry price minus exit price, times shares, gives (80-76.50) x 500 = $1,750 profit.

questions.q: What makes 'correlation-to-one' a strong answer to a question about a macro-shock risk scenario, rather than a generic answer like 'markets would be volatile'?
options: It names the specific mechanism — every position starts moving together in a broad shock, which is exactly when long/short diversification is weakest — rather than a vague statement
It avoids referencing any real market mechanism at all
It only applies to options positions, not equities
It guarantees the book will be unaffected by any macro event
questions.explain: Naming the specific mechanism (correlation-to-one, observed in SR-5's own COVID beta spike to ~0.25) demonstrates real understanding of why dollar-neutral books are vulnerable in broad macro shocks, not just generic caution.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a market order and a limit order?
options: A market order guarantees price but not execution; a limit order guarantees execution but not price
A market order guarantees execution but not price; a limit order guarantees price but not execution
Both guarantee the same price and execution outcome
Limit orders can only be used by market makers
questions.explain: A market order executes immediately at whatever price is available, while a limit order only executes at a specified price or better, potentially going unfilled.
